body:
You will learn to select and use grammar from context in the context of school life & education through age-appropriate sources about eco club meeting. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.1.G1: context clues, subject–verb agreement, time markers, tense choice, modal verbs and a final meaning check. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.1.G1. 4. Apply context clues, subject–verb agreement, time markers, tense choice, modal verbs and a final meaning check. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Context: Green School Fair. Source: 'The eco club meets beside the library at 14:40 on Tuesday. Members bring one reusable bottle and present a recycling idea.' Task: choose the grammatically accurate report. Solution: 'The group records the key detail before it presents the result.' The singular group takes records, and the time relationship remains consistent with the source.
- Worked example 2 — Context: Sports Team Notice. A learner writes, 'The students is preparing the activity.' Solution: 'The students are preparing the activity.' The plural subject requires are; the correction preserves the current preparation meaning rather than changing the tense.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the G1 result against meaning and form.

- Can I apply ENG.7.1.G1 to a new source and cite the clue I used?
- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.1.G1 develops the ability to select and use grammar from context in the context of school life & education. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific G1 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

All evidence needed for these examples is supplied in text. A future visual or audio stimulus must be bound to its exact task; no decorative image is used and no caption or alt text may reveal the answer.

body:
You will learn to prepare for reading and predict content in the context of school life & education through age-appropriate sources about eco club meeting. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.1.R1: heading and layout clues, prior knowledge, a provisional reading prediction and later verification. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.1.R1. 4. Apply heading and layout clues, prior knowledge, a provisional reading prediction and later verification. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Before using the text titled 'Green School Fair', predict that it may explain eco club meeting. Solution: keep the prediction provisional, then use the source 'The eco club meets beside the library at 14:40 on Tuesday. Members bring one reusable bottle and present a recycling idea.' to confirm the topic and revise any unsupported detail.
- Worked example 2 — A learner predicts an unrelated weather report from the title 'Sports Team Notice'. Solution: replace that guess with a prediction about basketball schedule change, then verify it against 'Basketball practice moves to the small gym on Friday because the main hall hosts a concert. Players arrive at 16:10 with indoor shoes.'. A prediction guides attention but never replaces the source.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the R1 result against meaning and form.

- Can I apply ENG.7.1.R1 to a new source and cite the clue I used?
- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.1.R1 develops the ability to prepare for reading and predict content in the context of school life & education. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific R1 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.1.R2. 4. Apply skimming for gist, scanning for a key word, close reading for detail and source-based confirmation. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Source: 'The eco club meets beside the library at 14:40 on Tuesday. Members bring one reusable bottle and present a recycling idea.' Task: find one exact supporting detail. Solution: record '14:40 on Tuesday'. Use this wording because it is explicitly stated; do not add a time, place or action that the source does not provide.

Strategy: scan for relevant key words, then check the full sentence. Solution: note 'small gym at 16:10'. The nearby words confirm the detail and prevent a familiar but unrelated word from controlling the answer.

Core concepts for ENG.7.1.R3: classification criteria, comparison, linked textual clues and an inference that stays within the text. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

- Worked example 1 — Source: 'The eco club meets beside the library at 14:40 on Tuesday. Members bring one reusable bottle and present a recycling idea.' Solution: identify the shared topic as basketball schedule change, then state which action or condition differs. Classification names a common criterion; inference explains a supported relationship rather than guessing a hidden fact.

- Worked example 1 — In 'The eco club meets beside the library at 14:40 on Tuesday. Members bring one reusable bottle and present a recycling idea.', infer the contextual meaning of 'reusable'. body:
You will learn to draft a clear written text in the context of school life & education through age-appropriate sources about eco club meeting. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.1.W3: a complete draft with clear reference, source-based detail, coherent order and reader action. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.1.W3. 4. Apply a complete draft with clear reference, source-based detail, coherent order and reader action. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Writing task: create a short text for 'Green School Fair'. Solution: apply a complete draft with clear reference, source-based detail, coherent order and reader action. Use the source detail '14:40 on Tuesday', organise it for the intended reader, and check that every sentence supports eco club meeting rather than adding an unrelated claim.
- Worked example 2 — Draft about 'Sports Team Notice': one sentence is vague and a key condition is missing. Solution: replace the vague wording with 'practice', restore 'small gym at 16:10', revise the order and mechanics, and compare the final text with the source before sharing.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the W3 result against meaning and form.

- Can I apply ENG.7.1.W3 to a new source and cite the clue I used?
- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.1.W3 develops the ability to draft a clear written text in the context of school life & education. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific W3 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

- Worked example 1 — Read the detail 'every test is repeated twice'. Solution: stress the main action and the time or place, pronounce final sounds completely, and pause between information groups. This delivery makes the source meaning easier to follow without changing any words.

You will learn to classify, compare and infer meaning while reading in the context of classroom life & learning through age-appropriate sources about a controlled classroom test. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.2.R3: classification criteria, comparison, linked textual clues and an inference that stays within the text. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.2.R3. 4. Apply classification criteria, comparison, linked textual clues and an inference that stays within the text. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Source: 'Each group hangs equal masses from three paper strips. It records the greatest mass each strip holds and repeats every test twice.' Solution: classify it as a controlled classroom test and infer that the actions form one connected plan. The inference uses several linked details and does not claim that the plan applies to every setting.
- Worked example 2 — Compare the evidence in 'First read your partner's paragraph silently. Next underline one clear detail, and finally suggest one question the reader still has.'. Solution: identify the shared topic as peer review steps, then state which action or condition differs. Classification names a common criterion; inference explains a supported relationship rather than guessing a hidden fact.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the R3 result against meaning and form.

- Can I apply ENG.7.2.R3 to a new source and cite the clue I used?
- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.2.R3 develops the ability to classify, compare and infer meaning while reading in the context of classroom life & learning. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific R3 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

Core concepts for ENG.7.2.R4: a named reading strategy, the evidence it revealed, a remaining difficulty and a realistic next step. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

- Worked example 1 — After the reading task on 'Testing Paper Strength', write: 'I identified a controlled classroom test and verified every test is repeated twice, but I need to check the section containing repeat once more.' This reflection names evidence, a gap and a next action.

Core concepts for ENG.7.3.S4: turn-taking, clarification, confirmation, polite disagreement and repair of misunderstanding. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

You will learn to select and use vocabulary from context in the context of personal life & well-being through age-appropriate sources about an evening well-being routine. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.3.V1: nearby words, topic, collocation, word family, contextual meaning and dictionary confirmation. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

- Worked example 1 — In 'Eda finishes her snack at 18:00, cycles for half an hour, prepares her school bag, and keeps screens outside the bedroom after 21:15.', infer the contextual meaning of 'balanced'. Solution: connect it with an evening well-being routine and the nearby actions, propose a meaning, then confirm it in a dictionary. Context narrows meaning; it does not make every guess correct.
- Worked example 2 — In 'Kerem fills a 750-millilitre bottle before school, drinks some at every break, and records whether any water remains at 15:30.', a learner selects an unrelated meaning for 'hydration'. Solution: examine its collocation and word family in the sentence, choose the meaning linked with a daily water plan, and test whether that meaning keeps the whole sentence coherent.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the V1 result against meaning and form.

body:
You will learn to classify, compare and infer meaning while listening in the context of life in the neighbourhood & city and social life through age-appropriate sources about a community repair event. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.5.L3: classification criteria, comparison, linked listening details and evidence-limited inference. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.5.L3. 4. Apply classification criteria, comparison, linked listening details and evidence-limited inference. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Source: 'Volunteers inspect broken small items at the community centre from 11:00 to 14:00. Visitors register online and carry their own replacement parts.' Solution: classify it as a community repair event and infer that the actions form one connected plan. The inference uses several linked details and does not claim that the plan applies to every setting.
- Worked example 2 — Compare the evidence in 'The youth council compares lighting on three routes, marks two dark corners, and recommends the path with working lamps and a pedestrian crossing.'. Solution: identify the shared topic as a neighbourhood safety study, then state which action or condition differs. Classification names a common criterion; inference explains a supported relationship rather than guessing a hidden fact.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the L3 result against meaning and form.

- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Core concepts for ENG.7.5.P1: content-word stress, complete final sounds, meaningful pauses, phrasing and intonation linked to purpose. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

- Worked example 1 — Read the detail 'community centre from 11:00 to 14:00'. Solution: stress the main action and the time or place, pronounce final sounds completely, and pause between information groups. This delivery makes the source meaning easier to follow without changing any words.

body:
You will learn to identify the listening topic and key details in the context of life in the world & culture through age-appropriate sources about a cross-cultural postcard exchange. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.6.L2: listening topic, signal words, speaker purpose, stated detail and concise note-taking. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.6.L2. 4. Apply listening topic, signal words, speaker purpose, stated detail and concise note-taking. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — Source: 'Partner classes exchange postcards about a daily custom. Each card explains the custom, avoids stereotypes, and asks one respectful question.' Task: find one exact supporting detail. Solution: record 'ask one respectful question'. Use this wording because it is explicitly stated; do not add a time, place or action that the source does not provide.
- Worked example 2 — Source: 'Groups research where one dish is eaten, identify two main ingredients, and cite the museum or cultural source used for the description.' body:
You will learn to reflect on and share the speaking process in the context of life in the world & culture through age-appropriate sources about a cross-cultural postcard exchange. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.6.S6: a specific strength, evidence of a speaking difficulty and an actionable improvement target. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.6.S6. 4. Apply a specific strength, evidence of a speaking difficulty and an actionable improvement target. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — After the speaking task on 'Postcards Across Cultures', write: 'I identified a cross-cultural postcard exchange and verified ask one respectful question, but I need to check the section containing custom once more.' This reflection names evidence, a gap and a next action.
- Worked example 2 — Weak reflection: 'It was good.' Improved solution: 'In the World Food Exhibit task I used cite the description source accurately, but my explanation of source was unclear; next time I will mark and rehearse that point.' The revision is specific and testable.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the S6 result against meaning and form.

- Can I apply ENG.7.6.S6 to a new source and cite the clue I used?
- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.6.S6 develops the ability to reflect on and share the speaking process in the context of life in the world & culture. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific S6 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

body:
You will learn to select and use vocabulary from context in the context of life in the world & culture through age-appropriate sources about a cross-cultural postcard exchange. You will identify relevant evidence, apply the target English process and explain how the source supports your response.

Core concepts for ENG.7.6.V1: nearby words, topic, collocation, word family, contextual meaning and dictionary confirmation. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Activate familiar English words and experiences, but keep every prediction provisional. Distinguish a source detail from your own idea, and use English word order, reference and punctuation when you communicate the result.

1. Identify the purpose and audience. 2. Preview the source. 3. Locate evidence relevant to ENG.7.6.V1. 4. Apply nearby words, topic, collocation, word family, contextual meaning and dictionary confirmation. 5. Compare alternatives. 6. Check meaning and form. 7. Revise after feedback.

- Worked example 1 — In 'Partner classes exchange postcards about a daily custom. Each card explains the custom, avoids stereotypes, and asks one respectful question.', infer the contextual meaning of 'custom'. Solution: connect it with a cross-cultural postcard exchange and the nearby actions, propose a meaning, then confirm it in a dictionary. Context narrows meaning; it does not make every guess correct.
- Worked example 2 — In 'Groups research where one dish is eaten, identify two main ingredients, and cite the museum or cultural source used for the description.', a learner selects an unrelated meaning for 'source'. Solution: examine its collocation and word family in the sentence, choose the meaning linked with a sourced cultural exhibit, and test whether that meaning keeps the whole sentence coherent.

Common mistakes include ignoring the source, translating word for word, selecting an option because of one familiar word, confusing prediction with fact, omitting the audience, and failing to check the V1 result against meaning and form.

- Can I explain why one plausible alternative is unsupported?
- Can I revise my response after checking meaning, form, purpose and audience?

Outcome ENG.7.6.V1 develops the ability to select and use vocabulary from context in the context of life in the world & culture. A strong response uses source evidence, applies the specific V1 process, communicates clearly in English and states any limit on the conclusion.

Core concepts for ENG.7.6.W1: audience, purpose, relevant source evidence, text type, plan and success criteria. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Core concepts for ENG.7.7.L3: classification criteria, comparison, linked listening details and evidence-limited inference. These concepts are used together; a familiar word or an attractive option cannot replace source meaning, audience, language form or task purpose.

Solution: classify it as a low-impact bird survey and infer that the actions form one connected plan. The inference uses several linked details and does not claim that the plan applies to every setting.
- Worked example 2 — Compare the evidence in 'Students collect no plants. They compare soil moisture at two approved points, photograph the ground, and return every loose stone to its place.'. Solution: identify the shared topic as a careful forest observation, then state which action or condition differs.
